opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the core issue is that the security model we've inherited for software just doesn't map well onto what agents actually do. Traditionally you have fairly static permissions: this user can read this table, this service can call this API. That works when a human is in the loop making each decision, or when the program's behavior is fixed and you can reason about it ahead of time.

With a coding agent, neither of those holds. The agent is taking actions on your behalf, often many of them in a row, and what it does depends on the input it reads along the way: a README, an issue someone filed, a web page, the output of a tool. Any of those can contain instructions, and the agent can't always tell data from commands. That's the prompt injection problem. If you give the agent a static, broad permission set, like "you can run shell commands and you have my GitHub token," then whatever ends up in its context effectively inherits all of that power.

So the question becomes: is this action OK *given what the agent is doing right now and where the request came from*? Pushing to a branch might be fine when the user asked for a bug fix. It's very different if the agent just read an untrusted issue comment and is now trying to send your environment variables to some external URL. Same capability, completely different risk. A static policy can't express that difference. A contextual one can, by looking at the task, the provenance of the data, and the flow of information. Did secret data touch untrusted output? Is this action consistent with the user's intent?

There's also a usability side. If you lock everything down, the agent asks for approval every thirty seconds, people get approval fatigue, and they either click "yes" without reading or turn on the YOLO mode. That's arguably worse. Contextual policies let you be permissive where the risk is low and strict exactly where it matters, so the human only gets involved for the decisions that are actually consequential.

And I think this is really a systems problem more than a model problem. You can make models more robust to injection, and that helps, but you don't want your security guarantees to depend on the model never making a mistake. You want something like what we do in databases or operating systems: track information flow, enforce policies at the boundary where the agent touches real resources, and keep audit logs so you can reason about what happened afterward. The model can be smart and still be wrong sometimes. The policy layer is what makes it safe to give it real power.

r001.rationale: The response explains that broad permissions can let an agent use information from its context to send secrets to an external destination, and contrasts the risk of the same capability across contexts. This conveys how individually available read and publish capabilities can combine to leak data.

r002.rationale: The response says policy should consider what the agent is doing now, where the request came from, and the information flow, illustrating an action after reading an untrusted issue. This makes permission depend on prior activity in the session.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short version is that the permission model we inherited from operating systems and from earlier automation just doesn't match what an agent actually does.

When you give a human engineer access to a repo and a shell, you're not really granting them a fixed list of allowed commands. You're trusting their judgment in context. They know that running the test suite is fine, that `rm -rf` on a build directory is fine, and that the same command on the production data directory is absolutely not fine, even though syntactically it's the same operation. A coding agent is now doing that same class of work, and if all you can express is "this tool is allowed" or "this tool is denied," you end up in one of two bad places. Either you lock it down so tightly that it can't accomplish anything without stopping to ask every thirty seconds, and people just rubber-stamp approvals, or you open it up and hope for the best.

The thing that makes it hard is that the right answer depends on things that aren't visible in the action itself. Which branch am I on? Is this a scratch directory or something checked in? Did the instruction to do this come from the user, or did it show up inside a file I was reading? That last one matters a lot. Agents read untrusted content constantly: issue threads, READMEs, dependency source, web pages. If a policy can't distinguish "the user asked me to push this" from "a comment in the code told me to push this," you have an injection problem that no static allowlist will solve.

So what I mean by contextual policy is roughly three things. First, policies should be conditioned on state, not just on the action, so the same command can be allowed in one directory and require confirmation in another. Second, they should track provenance, where an instruction came from, and treat that as a first-class input. And third, they should be legible to the agent itself. If the agent understands why something is gated, it can plan around it, batch up the risky steps, and ask once with a clear explanation rather than fumbling through a sequence of denials.

The analogy I keep coming back to is data governance. We spent years learning that access control on tables wasn't enough; you needed row-level and column-level policies, lineage, and audit, because the question "should this person see this data" depended on context. Agents are going to force the same evolution on code execution. The alternative, where safety is just a wall of prompts the user clicks through, isn't really safety. It's just friction with a false sense of control.

r001.rationale: The response discusses agents reading untrusted content and the risk of being instructed to push, but it does not explain how separately legitimate access to confidential documents and permission to publish externally can combine to leak data.

r002.rationale: The response says policies should depend on state and instruction provenance, but it does not describe permissions depending on earlier actions in the same session.

astra-6.text:
I think the key issue is that coding agents need fairly broad access to be useful. They need to read code, run commands, install dependencies, and sometimes interact with services. But whether an action is safe depends a lot on the task. Sending a request to a server might be necessary for testing an integration, or it might be leaking a credential. You can’t distinguish those cases just by looking at the tool being called.

And these agents are reading things that you don’t necessarily trust: repository files, issue descriptions, dependency documentation. Those can contain instructions that try to steer the agent away from what the user asked it to do. So you want policies that take into account what the user actually authorized, what data the agent is accessing, and where that data is going.

The goal is to let the agent do useful work autonomously while keeping its authority bounded by the task. Otherwise, you end up either giving it too much access or asking the user to approve every little step.

r001.rationale: The response mentions broad access and possible credential leakage, but it does not explain that combining access to confidential documents with external publishing can leak data even when each permission is individually legitimate.

r002.rationale: The response says policies should consider authorization, accessed data, and destination, but does not say permissions depend on earlier actions in the same session.

sol-6.1.text:
Because a coding agent needs to do things that would look dangerous under a blanket security policy. It needs to run code, install dependencies, and sometimes access credentials or services. But whether those actions are appropriate depends on what the user actually asked it to do.

For example, reading a credential to deploy an application might be legitimate. Reading that same credential because some text in a repository told the agent to upload it somewhere is very different. The tool operation could look identical, but the purpose and destination matter.

So you need policies that take that context into account: what task is authorized, what resources it requires, and where information is allowed to go. And you want those policies enforced outside the agent itself, because the agent is processing untrusted material. That lets you give it enough access to be useful while still putting boundaries around what it can do.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts legitimate credential use with an unauthorized upload, but does not clearly explain how separately legitimate access to confidential documents and external publishing can combine to cause data leakage.

r002.rationale: It says permissions should depend on the task, resources, and destination, but does not describe permissions changing based on earlier actions in the same session.
